fatal_errors: The proposed method omits the central experimental approach: in situ heating under vacuum coupled with aberration-corrected STEM/STEM-EDS; molecular dynamics was only a complementary method.
Periodic boundary conditions and an NVT bulk-like setup are poorly matched to isolated sub-10 nm nanoparticles where free surfaces, segregation, reshaping, melting, and evaporation are decisive.
The predicted enhanced thermal stability contradicts the observed poor stability, active diffusion, Au/Cu surface segregation, evaporation, and particle-size reduction.
An increase in mean squared displacement is interpreted incorrectly as evidence of enhanced thermal stability; it instead indicates increased atomic mobility.
The Kawasaki exchange mechanism, quantitative MSD increase, simulation duration, and falsification thresholds are asserted without evidence.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses atomic-scale heating of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles and correctly invokes atomistic simulation and thermally activated diffusion, so it has limited topical alignment. However, it fails to reconstruct the key method and rationale: temperature-resolved, aberration-corrected in situ STEM/STEM-EDS under vacuum directly tracks morphology and elemental redistribution, while molecular dynamics explains self-diffusion and shape-dependent segregation. It also misses the governing surface-energy mechanism, especially Au and Cu enrichment at free surfaces, and reaches the opposite conclusion about thermal stability. The proposed MSD-based test cannot distinguish entropy-stabilized sluggish diffusion from kinetically controlled segregation and evaporation without composition-resolved surface and morphology measurements.
